Sumwalt said the cockpit voice recorder “shows nothing out of the ordinary” during preflight operations. He said the recording revealed that 41 seconds after the brakes were released, there were sounds of bumping and rattling. Four seconds later, a crew member called for a rejected takeoff.

Flight 1404 was taking off at about 6:18 p.m. Sumwalt said the plane reached a maximum speed of 119 knots, or 137 mph, before entering the ravine.

Continental spokeswoman Julie King, however, told CNN that she was unaware of any announcement about engine problems aboard the flight.

Sumwalt said the weather was clear and that there were no objects blocking the runway.

Thirty-eight people were hurt in the crash, most suffering bruises and broken bones as alarmed passengers attempted to escape a fire that started aboard Flight 1404. No one was killed.

According to Sumwalt, the captain, who had worked for Continental for 11 years, was injured and was “not physically able” to speak with investigators yet. However, an investigator did interview the first officer, who said the taxi and the beginning of the takeoff roll appeared normal.

The co-pilot then “noticed a deviation from the center line of the runway and a sudden left turn,” Sumwalt said.

Also on the plane was an off-duty crew that had flown the aircraft into Denver before its scheduled Saturday flight to Houston. The first officer from that earlier crew reported that there had been “absolutely no problem with the aircraft” during the preceding flight.

Sumwalt said the cockpit voice recorder revealed “nothing out of the ordinary” during preflight procedures. He said the recording showed that 41 seconds after the brakes were released, sounds of bumping and rattling could be heard. Four seconds after that, a crew member called for the takeoff to be aborted.

Flight 1404 was beginning its takeoff at about 6:18 p.m. Sumwalt said the plane reached a top speed of 119 knots, or 137 mph, before it ended up in the ravine.

**NTSB: Early evidence shows Continental jet’s engines were working before Denver runway crash**

**DENVER** — Federal investigators said Monday that early evidence from Continental Airlines Flight 1404 indicates the jet’s engines were producing power and its braking systems showed no obvious signs of failure before the aircraft veered off a runway at Denver International Airport and burst into flames.

The Boeing 737-500, bound for Houston, left the left side of Runway 34R during takeoff Saturday evening, skidding across uneven ground before coming to rest in a ravine-like area and catching fire. All 115 people aboard survived, though dozens were taken to hospitals with injuries ranging from broken bones to smoke inhalation.

Robert Sumwalt, a member of the National Transportation Safety Board, cautioned that investigators had not determined a cause and were still reviewing flight data, cockpit recordings, weather conditions and the actions of the flight crew.

“We are very early in this investigation,” Sumwalt said. “We will be looking at everything — the aircraft, the crew, the weather and the runway environment.”

Sumwalt said the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder had been recovered and sent to Washington for analysis. Early information, he said, suggested the aircraft accelerated normally before it suddenly departed the runway.

“There is no indication at this point of any engine failure,” Sumwalt said, adding that investigators had also found no immediate evidence of a brake malfunction.

Weather is expected to be a key focus. Investigators said Denver was experiencing strong, shifting winds around the time of the accident, including crosswinds that may have affected the aircraft during its takeoff roll. Sumwalt said the NTSB would compare tower wind readings, pilot reports and recorded aircraft data to determine what the crew encountered.

Passengers described a terrifying sequence as the plane began its takeoff roll and then abruptly lurched.

“It felt like we were going up, and then all of a sudden we were bouncing all over the place,” one passenger told reporters after escaping the burning aircraft. “Then there was fire outside the window.”

Another passenger said the aircraft appeared to sway violently before leaving the runway.

“It was like the plane just went sideways,” the passenger said. “People were screaming, and then when it stopped, everyone was trying to get out.”

Emergency slides were deployed as flames and thick smoke surrounded parts of the aircraft. Passengers said flight attendants shouted instructions and moved people quickly toward the exits.

“They kept yelling, ‘Leave everything, get out, get out,’” one passenger recalled. “You could feel the heat.”

The crash temporarily disrupted operations at Denver International Airport, one of the nation’s busiest hubs, but airport officials said the runway remained closed only while investigators documented the scene and crews removed wreckage.

Continental Airlines said it was cooperating fully with investigators and assisting passengers and their families. The airline identified the aircraft as operating Flight 1404 from Denver to Houston’s George Bush Intercontinental Airport.

Sumwalt stressed that the NTSB’s early observations should not be read as conclusions.

“We don’t jump to conclusions,” he said. “Our job is to gather the facts, analyze them carefully and determine what happened so we can help prevent it from happening again.”

**DENVER, Dec. 22, 2008** — Federal investigators on Monday continued examining why a Continental Airlines jet veered violently off a runway during takeoff at Denver International Airport, skidded into a ravine and burst into flames, injuring dozens but killing no one in what survivors described as a terrifying escape from a smoke-filled aircraft.

Continental Flight 1404, a Boeing 737-500 bound for Houston, was carrying **110 passengers and five crew members** when it departed the left side of **Runway 34R** shortly after 6 p.m. Saturday. The aircraft crossed rough ground, its landing gear sheared off, and it came to rest in a shallow gully several thousand feet from the runway before fire engulfed much of the fuselage.

Authorities said **38 people were injured**, with several requiring hospitalization for broken bones, burns, back injuries and smoke inhalation. No fatalities were reported. Emergency crews credited the survival of everyone aboard to the rapid evacuation of passengers and the response by airport firefighters, who arrived within minutes and fought flames burning through the right side of the aircraft.

The National Transportation Safety Board said the plane’s **flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder** had been recovered and sent to Washington for analysis. Investigators said early information showed both recorders appeared to contain usable data, including cockpit communications and technical information from the takeoff roll.

NTSB officials cautioned that no cause had been determined. Investigators were reviewing weather conditions, runway conditions, aircraft performance, crew actions and the jet’s mechanical systems. At the time of the crash, Denver was experiencing strong, shifting winds, and investigators were focusing in part on whether a gust or crosswind played a role in the aircraft’s sudden departure from the runway.

Survivors said the takeoff initially felt normal, then abruptly turned chaotic.

“It was like the plane just shot off to the side,” one passenger recalled. “There was a huge bump, then another, and then everything went dark and smoky. People were screaming, and you could feel the heat.”

Another passenger said the cabin filled quickly with smoke after the aircraft stopped. “The flight attendants were yelling for everyone to get out,” the passenger said. “We climbed over seats and out through the exits. When I got outside, I turned around and saw flames coming from the plane.”

Passengers described sliding down emergency chutes, stumbling through snow and dirt, and helping one another away from the burning aircraft. Some said they heard a loud bang or series of jolts before the plane came to rest. Others reported seeing fire outside the windows almost immediately after the crash.

Continental Airlines said it was cooperating fully with investigators and assisting passengers and families. The airline sent a response team to Denver and arranged transportation and lodging for those affected. The flight had been scheduled to travel from Denver to Houston’s George Bush Intercontinental Airport.

The aircraft, a twin-engine Boeing 737-500, was heavily damaged. Video and photographs from the scene showed the fuselage cracked and charred, with the right side and wing area severely burned. Investigators planned to document the wreckage before moving it to a secure location for further inspection.

NTSB investigators were also interviewing the cockpit crew, flight attendants, passengers, air traffic controllers and emergency responders. The agency said it would examine maintenance records, pilot training records and cockpit procedures, as well as the runway surface and any available radar and tower recordings.

Airport officials said the runway was closed after the crash while investigators surveyed tire marks, debris trails and the aircraft’s path after it left the pavement. Other runways remained open, though the accident caused delays during a busy holiday travel weekend.

The crash was one of the most serious runway accidents at Denver International Airport since it opened in 1995. Aviation officials said the absence of fatalities was remarkable given the fire and the extent of the damage.

A preliminary NTSB report was expected within weeks, but officials said a final determination of probable cause could take many months.
